summary: Defines a structure by which information servers exchange indices from their databases in the Common Indexing Protocol, along with the meanings of its headers. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: A labeled-list format that lets one library tell another what is on its shelves.

questions: how do servers exchange directory indexes
what is cip common indexing protocol
subtitle: Lets database servers exchange labeled search indexes to find information across systems.

tldr.problem: Information servers need to exchange indexes describing what records they hold so other servers can route searches to the right place, but existing index formats do not support incremental updates or fine-grained attribution of values to records.
tldr.mechanism: The tagged index object attaches identification numbers to data values, grouping values with the same tag as belonging to the same record, and supports full or incremental updates with add, delete, and replace operations.
tldr.outcome: Servers can exchange index information efficiently, enabling distributed directories like LDAP and Whois++ to direct queries to the most likely source of answers.

today: RFC 2654 is Experimental. It was never updated or obsoleted. The tagged index object enabled discussion of distributed directory indexing, but widespread adoption of LDAP and later directory protocols reduced the need for this particular format. It remains a stable reference for the Common Indexing Protocol.

sections.title: Introduction and the CIP Protocol
sections.content:
The Common Indexing Protocol (CIP) provides a way for information servers to distribute searches across multiple systems. RFC 2654 defines the Tagged Index Object, the data structure exchanged in CIP to describe what records a server holds. Unlike earlier index formats such as Centroid (from Whois++), the tagged index object explicitly connects data values to the records they belong to, and natively supports incremental updates—crucial for databases with millions of records where exchanging complete copies would waste bandwidth.

This specification applies to many kinds of information servers: X.500 DSAs, LDAP servers, Whois++ servers, and others that operate as part of a distributed directory. The goal is to let a server locate the most appropriate information server to forward a query to, based on index information it holds.
sections.plainLanguage: A mail service wants to know: which post office handles the zip code 90210? It asks nearby post offices for their index. Each post office sends back: 'Here's my list of zip codes and the number of people we serve.' The system uses those lists to route your letter to the right place.

sections.title: The Directory Systems Problem
sections.content:
LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) organizes information in a hierarchical tree called the Directory Information Tree. When an LDAP server receives a query about a part of the tree it does not hold (for example, a Swedish entry from a US server), it must refer the client to another server. Traditionally, each LDAP server is configured with the name of exactly one other server to contact. This is crude and inefficient.

X.500 DSAs use a protocol called Directory Shadowing (DISP) to copy entire portions of the tree between servers. This is expensive and aimed at replication and fault tolerance, not at efficient query routing. The tagged index object, by contrast, exchanges only summary information about what data exists, without replicating the data itself. It enables servers to build smart referrals without maintaining shadow copies.
sections.plainLanguage: A big hotel has desks in 10 cities. Without the index, the New York desk only knows to call the single 'home office' for questions. With the index, New York can say: 'Los Angeles handles West Coast requests,' and send the guest to the right desk.

sections.title: Structure and Agreement
sections.content:
Before two servers exchange a tagged index object, they must agree on terms: the index type ('x-tagged-index-1'), the base URL for referrals, the supplier and consumer addresses, the maximum interval between updates, and how to maintain consistency (complete, tag-based, or unique ID-based). The agreement also specifies whether the update is sent encrypted or signed—critical for sensitive directory information.

The tagged index object itself is a MIME payload, sent as application/cip-index-object, encoded in UTF-8. The payload is a series of lines, each assigning one or more attribute values (such as names, email addresses, or titles) to records via tag numbers. A tag is a number: all values with tag 1 belong to the same record, tag 2 values belong to a different record, and so on.
sections.plainLanguage: Two libraries sign a contract: 'You send me your catalog twice a month in encrypted email.' Then each entry in the catalog says: 'Books 1, 2, and 3 are all about history' (tag 1), and 'Books 4 and 5 are science' (tag 2).

sections.title: Tokenization and Incremental Updates
sections.content:
The tagged index object defines how text is split into tokens for searching. The TOKEN type splits on whitespace and '@' (useful for email and names); RFC822 adds '.' to the split characters (for email addresses); DNS splits at any non-alphanumeric character (for domain names); FULL stores the entire value without splitting. The schema for an index declares which tokenization type applies to each attribute.

After the first full update, a supplier server can send incremental updates containing only the changes: an Add Block for new records, a Delete Block for removed records, and an Update Block for changed records. The consistency method agreed in advance determines what information must be repeated in each block. Full consistency requires all tokens; tag-based consistency requires only changed tokens; unique ID consistency requires only a unique identifier plus the changed tokens.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine updating the post office list. The first time you send the complete list. Next month, instead of rewriting everything, you just send: 'Add these 5 new zip codes' and 'Remove this 1 old one.' The post office knows to keep the rest as is.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The aggregate index may contain sensitive information about organizational structure or data. Server administrators must choose what to include. The spec allows several methods to protect the update in transit: PGP/MIME, S/MIME, SSLv3, or Fortezza. For distribution outside an enterprise, SSL with certificate verification is recommended.

Tokenization is a privacy tool: by breaking a name into tokens, a server can obscure complete names while still allowing searches. The protocol does not provide protection against spoofing or eavesdropping on its own; secure transport or signing must be applied. Information Server developers should support facilities to hide organizational structure when generating the index from the underlying database.
sections.plainLanguage: If you send library catalogs over the internet, encrypt them so no one else can read the list of books. And if the catalog says 'patron record 1 borrowed this book,' don't send the patron's full name—just a code number, so the other library learns what the person borrowed but not who they are.
